html:
The big picture

Kinematics says where the robot goes; dynamics says why it moves — which forces and torques the motors must produce. For rotating joints every linear quantity has a rotational twin: force ↔ torque, mass ↔ moment of inertia, so F = ma becomes T = J\alpha. With that you can compute the torque that holds an arm still (statics) or accelerates it (dynamics). Producing that torque reliably is the job of the controller: an open-loop controller just sends a command, while a closed-loop controller measures the output, compares it with the reference, and acts on the error. The standard closed-loop law is the PID controller (proportional, integral, derivative), which trades speed against overshoot. A good controller drives the error to zero while being robust, stable, smooth and responsive, and it sits at the bottom of a hierarchy: mission planning → motion planning (path, trajectory) → robot control.

Recap

  • Kinematics vs. dynamics
  • Types of links and joints
  • Degrees of freedom
  • The 3 main operations in coordinate transformation (translation, rotation, scaling)
  • Kinematic chain example: derive the forward kinematics of the 3-DoF planar manipulator with three revolute joints (H. Harry Asada, Introduction to Robotics) — see 5 Coordinate Transformation and Kinematics.

Dynamics

What is dynamics?

  • Dynamics provides a description of why things move.
  • It considers the physical impact (forces, torque) generated in or applied on the robotic system.

A robot is a very complex multi-body system (several links connected through actuators). For a robot with a fixed base, the dynamics may be formulated as ("don't worry about that (for now)"):

M(q)\,\ddot{q} + b(q, \dot{q}) + g(q) = \tau + J_c(q)^\top F_c
SymbolMeaning
M(q) \in \mathbb{R}^{n_q \times n_q}generalized mass matrix (printed: "orthogonal")
q, \dot{q}, \ddot{q} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_q}generalized position, velocity and acceleration vectors (joint angles and their derivatives)
b(q, \dot{q}) \in \mathbb{R}^{n_q}Coriolis and centrifugal terms
g(q) \in \mathbb{R}^{n_q}gravitational terms
\tau \in \mathbb{R}^{n_q}external generalized forces (the joint torques)
F_c \in \mathbb{R}^{n_c}external Cartesian forces (e.g. from contacts)
J_c(q) \in \mathbb{R}^{n_c \times n_q}geometric Jacobian corresponding to the external forces
Symbols
  • n_q — the number of joints (generalized coordinates); n_c — the number of external Cartesian force components
  • \mathbb{R}^{n_q} — a vector with n_q real entries; \mathbb{R}^{n_c \times n_q} — a matrix with n_c rows and n_q columns
  • \dot{q}, \ddot{q} — first and second time derivative of q (joint velocities and accelerations)
  • ^\top — the transpose (rows and columns swapped); J_c^\top turns Cartesian forces into joint torques
Unclear (slide 4)

The mass matrix is labelled "(orthogonal)". A mass matrix is symmetric and positive definite, not orthogonal (an orthogonal matrix is a rotation/reflection, M^\top M = I). Likely a slip in the source table.

Intuition

Read the big equation as F = ma for the whole arm, one row per joint: "mass × acceleration" (M\ddot{q}) plus the forces that appear only because the links swing around (b: centrifugal and Coriolis) plus gravity (g) must be supplied by the motor torques (\tau) and whatever pushes on the robot from outside (J_c^\top F_c). The mass matrix depends on q because a stretched-out arm is harder to rotate than a folded one.

Forces

What forces do you know?

  • weight (m \cdot g),
  • friction, normal force,
  • linear acceleration (m \cdot a),
  • rotary movement (centripetal acceleration),
  • Coriolis force,
  • electrical, magnetic, fluid/gas, thermal and atomic forces — compare to the types of actuators.

Linear and rotary motion

Linear motionRotary motion
displacementangle
linear velocityangular velocity
linear accelerationangular acceleration
massinertia
forcetorque
momentumangular momentum
F = m aT = J \alpha
p = m vL = I \omega

The slides use both J and I for the moment of inertia.

Why does inertia depend on where the mass is, not just how much there is?

A point mass m at distance r from the axis moves on a circle with speed v = r\omega and needs a force m a = m r \alpha to speed up; that force acts with lever arm r, so the torque is T = (m r^2)\,\alpha. The factor r enters twice — once because far-out mass has to move faster, once because the lever arm is longer. Adding up all mass elements gives J = \int r^2\,dm. So mass far from the axis counts quadratically: that's why a long stretched-out arm is so much harder to swing.

Statics example

Consider the following 1-DoF robot: a beam of mass m = 10\,\mathrm{kg} and length L = 1\,\mathrm{m}, pivoted at one end, with a mass m_1 = 3\,\mathrm{kg} hanging at the other end; g \approx 10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}. What torque T is necessary to keep the robot in place?

Dynamics example

Same robot. What torque T is necessary to accelerate the robot with \alpha = 1\,\mathrm{s^{-2}} in the counter-clockwise (ccw) direction? Hint: treat the beam as a long thin rod, and m_1 as a point mass.

J = \int_m r^2\,dm, \qquad \text{for a uniform distribution of mass: } J = \rho \int_V r^2\,dV
Symbols
  • J — moment of inertia about the rotation axis (kg·m²) (called I in other courses)
  • dm — a tiny piece of the body's mass (kg); \int_m — add up over all pieces of the body
  • r — distance of that piece from the rotation axis (m)
  • \rho — the (constant) density (kg/m³); dV — a tiny piece of volume (m³), so dm = \rho\,dV
Worked example — slides 7 and 8, holding and accelerating the 1-DoF arm
  1. Gravity torques about the pivot (force × lever arm): the beam's weight acts at its centre, L/2; the end mass at L.
T_g = m g \tfrac{L}{2} + m_1 g L = 10 \cdot 10 \cdot 0.5 + 3 \cdot 10 \cdot 1 = 50 + 30 = 80\,\mathrm{N\,m}
  1. Statics: to hold the arm still the motor must cancel this exactly: T = 80\,\mathrm{N\,m} (ccw, against gravity's clockwise pull).
  2. Inertia about the pivot: rod about its end \tfrac{1}{3} m L^2 = \tfrac{10}{3}, point mass m_1 L^2 = 3, so J = 6.33\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}.
  3. Dynamics: the motor must still beat gravity, and on top supply J\alpha:
T = T_g + J\alpha = 80 + 6.33 \cdot 1 \approx 86.3\,\mathrm{N\,m}

Symbols: T_g — torque needed against gravity (N·m); m, L — mass and length of the beam; m_1 — end mass; g — gravitational acceleration; J — moment of inertia about the pivot (kg·m²); \alpha — angular acceleration (rad/s²); T — motor torque.

Note how small the acceleration part is here: most of the torque of a horizontal arm goes into fighting gravity.

Common mistake

Putting the whole beam mass at the end (m L instead of m \tfrac{L}{2} for the weight, or m L^2 instead of \tfrac{1}{3} m L^2 for the inertia). A uniform beam's weight acts at its centre, and its inertia about one end is \tfrac{1}{3} m L^2 — the mass is spread out, most of it closer than L. Only the point mass m_1 sits fully at distance L.

Inertia

E_{\mathrm{kin}} = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2 \quad\longrightarrow\quad E_{\mathrm{rot}} = \tfrac{1}{2} m r^2 \omega^2, \qquad J = \int_m r^2\,dm
Symbols
  • E_{\mathrm{kin}} — kinetic energy of a moving mass (J); m — mass (kg); v — speed (m/s)
  • E_{\mathrm{rot}} — rotational kinetic energy (J); r — distance from the axis (m); \omega — angular velocity (rad/s), using v = r\omega
  • J — moment of inertia (kg·m²), as above

(For a point mass m r^2 = J, so in general E_{\mathrm{rot}} = \tfrac{1}{2} J \omega^2.)

Why is a rod \tfrac{1}{12} m l^2 about its centre but \tfrac{1}{3} m l^2 about its end?

About the end, more of the mass is far from the axis (up to a full l away), and far mass counts with r^2. The parallel-axis theorem links the two: moving the axis a distance d away from the centre of mass adds m d^2. For the rod, d = l/2: \tfrac{1}{12} m l^2 + m \left(\tfrac{l}{2}\right)^2 = \tfrac{1}{12} m l^2 + \tfrac{3}{12} m l^2 = \tfrac{1}{3} m l^2.

Dynamics of a robot arm

  • q = [q_1, q_2, q_3, \dots, q_n] correspond to the joint angles; \dot{q} is the corresponding velocity, \ddot{q} the corresponding acceleration.
  • Generalized: in the rotational domain (r, \varphi, z) vs. Cartesian (x, y, z).

  • In M(q)\ddot{q} + b(q,\dot{q}) + g(q) = \tau + J_c(q)^\top F_c:

    • M(q)\ddot{q} generalizes F = m a and T = J\alpha;
    • b(q, \dot{q}) holds the Coriolis and centrifugal forces: F_{\mathrm{cen}} = m v^2 / r, F_{\mathrm{cor}} = -2 m (\vec{\omega} \times \vec{v});
    • g(q) holds gravity, F_G = m g (only effective in the "vertical" direction);
    • \tau + J_c^\top F_c: external forces in generalized form \tau or Cartesian form F_c. J_c is called a Jacobian matrix and is used for mapping between different domains.
Connection

The Jacobian is the missing piece behind the third key question of 5 Coordinate Transformation and Kinematics ("what is the Cartesian velocity for a set of rotating motors?"): it maps joint velocities to tool velocities, and — transposed, as here — tool forces back to joint torques. Near a singularity (4 Operation, Simulation and Communication of Robots) this mapping breaks down.

Link to control

A robot travels from a point P_1 to a point P_2. What do we need to provide?

  • the joint angles to reach P_2 and a set of convenient intermediate points (path planning — covered later — and trajectory);
  • the speed, to determine how fast we go (again, Cartesian velocities have to be mapped into the rotational domain), or the allowed time period;
  • (acceleration, jerk);
  • the necessary forces to keep the robot moving (torque).

What does our motor get as input?

  • voltage, current (electrical power),
  • other analog or digital input.

How do we translate the information? How do we make sure that the robot does "what it is told to do"? → the controller.

Types of control

Questions on the slide: Can you name examples of open/closed-loop controllers? What is the difference in behaviour? Which one is preferred for operation in robots?

Worked example — answering slide 12
  1. Open-loop examples: a toaster or washing machine running on a timer, a stepper motor driven by counting steps without an encoder (3 Actuators). The controller never checks the result.
  2. Closed-loop examples: a room thermostat, a car's cruise control, a servo motor with an encoder. The controller measures the output and corrects.
  3. Behaviour: open loop is simple and cheap but cannot notice disturbances (a heavier load, a slope, a lost step) — errors go uncorrected. Closed loop corrects disturbances and model errors, at the cost of a sensor and the risk of instability if tuned badly.
  4. For robots: closed loop, because loads, friction and environments change, and position errors accumulate otherwise.

Introduction to robot control

What are the components of a control system?

  1. Input
  2. Process being controlled
  3. Output
  4. Sensing elements
  5. Controller and actuating devices

Find examples for each part.

Closed-loop control example — thermostat

The temperature controller for your living room is set to T = 23\,^\circ\mathrm{C}. What is the reference? What does your controller do? Why do we even need closed-loop control? What effects can alter the output (room temperature)?

Worked example — the thermostat as a control loop
  1. Reference r: the set temperature, 23\,^\circ\mathrm{C}.
  2. Sensor → estimate y: the thermometer in the room.
  3. Error: e = r - y; at 21\,^\circ\mathrm{C} measured, e = +2\,^\circ\mathrm{C}.
  4. Controller → control signal u: opens the heating valve / supplies current to the heater, more for a bigger error.
  5. System (plant): the room — walls, air, windows — which turns heating power into temperature, slowly.
  6. Disturbances that make closed loop necessary: an open window, outside temperature, sunshine, people and devices giving off heat. A fixed (open-loop) heater setting would be right for only one of these situations.

What a controller does

  • It maps an input (desired room temperature) to an output (supplied current to the electrical heater / valve of your heating cycle).
  • It needs to consider the capabilities/restrictions of your system (actuator) or environment.
  • It needs to apply a control scheme — essentially how to ramp to the desired temperature (PID, or any sub-combination).
  • It needs a certain tolerance level (e.g. for 23\,^\circ\mathrm{C}: what does it do at 23.1\,^\circ\mathrm{C} or 22.9\,^\circ\mathrm{C}?) → a set of logical rules.
  • It may need to consider different modes (e.g. fast heating or energy saver). We call these states.
  • It may need to consider external influences (e.g. how to behave with an open window or door).
  • Your controller detects an increasing mismatch in room temperature (window fully open in winter). How should it react?
Intuition

The open-window question is about the controller's limits: no amount of heating reaches 23\,^\circ\mathrm{C} with the window open in winter, and a controller that just keeps raising its output (the integral part, below, keeps growing) wastes energy and overshoots badly once the window closes. A sensible controller detects the situation (temperature falling fast despite full heating) and switches state — for example, pauses heating until the window is closed.

What's a PID controller?

  • Your thermostat is set to 25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}, but your room is at 20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}. Your controller wants to react as fast as possible and sets the target directly to 25\,^\circ\mathrm{C} (blue curve).
  • That's where a PID controller kicks in: it transforms the sharp transition of the input into a "softer" one.
  • Heating as fast as possible may cause an overshoot and trick your controller into needing to cool down again.
  • Ever driven a car? You approach a crossing and the traffic light is red — how do you adjust your velocity? Or: you just made it onto the Autobahn — how do you adjust your throttle?
  • P … proportional, I … integral, D … derivative.
  • The controller considers the first derivative and the integral of your control variable.
  • Do these curves look familiar? Hint: a damper in a car (mass–spring–damper).

PID controller

Derivation (single mass), from the sum of forces on the mass:

\sum F = -k x - c \dot{x} + F_{\mathrm{external}} = m \ddot{x}
Symbols
  • \sum F — the total force on the mass (N)
  • k — spring constant (N/m); x — displacement of the mass (m)
  • c — damping coefficient (N·s/m); \dot{x} — velocity (m/s)
  • F_{\mathrm{external}} — the applied (e.g. motor/controller) force (N)
  • m — mass (kg); \ddot{x} — acceleration (m/s²)

Rearranged into the standard form:

\ddot{x} + 2 \zeta \omega_n \dot{x} + \omega_n^2 x = u, \qquad \omega_n = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}, \quad \zeta = \frac{c}{2 m \omega_n}, \quad u = \frac{F_{\mathrm{external}}}{m}
Symbols
  • \omega_n — undamped natural frequency (rad/s): how fast the system would oscillate without damping
  • \zeta — damping ratio (zeta, dimensionless): \zeta < 1 oscillates (underdamped), \zeta = 1 critically damped, \zeta > 1 creeps back (overdamped)
  • u — the input: external force per mass (m/s²)
  • k, m, c — spring constant, mass, damping coefficient, as above

\omega_n is the undamped natural frequency and \zeta the damping ratio. The homogeneous equation \ddot{x} + 2\zeta\omega_n\dot{x} + \omega_n^2 x = 0 has the solution

x = A e^{-\omega_n t \left(\zeta + \sqrt{\zeta^2 - 1}\right)} + B e^{-\omega_n t \left(\zeta - \sqrt{\zeta^2 - 1}\right)}
Symbols
  • A, B — constants fixed by the starting conditions (initial position and velocity)
  • e — Euler's number; t — time (s)
  • \omega_n, \zeta — natural frequency and damping ratio, as above

If \zeta < 1, then \zeta^2 - 1 is negative, so the square root is imaginary and the solution has an oscillatory component. (The slide's plot shows the response of such a system with K_p = 1, K_i = 0, K_d = 0: it settles well below the reference of 1.)

Intuition — what P, I and D each do

With error e(t) = r - y, the PID control signal is u(t) = K_p\,e(t) + K_i \int_0^t e\,d\tau + K_d\,\dot{e}(t). (r — reference (desired value); y — measured/estimated output; u(t) — control signal; K_p, K_i, K_d — proportional, integral and derivative gains; \tau — just the integration variable over past time, not torque; \dot{e} — rate of change of the error.)

  • P — the present: push in proportion to how far off you are. Bigger K_p = faster, but more overshoot.
  • I — the past: add up the error over time. Any lasting small error keeps growing the integral until it is gone — this removes the steady-state offset.
  • D — the future: react to how fast the error is changing, braking before you arrive. It acts like the damper c and reduces overshoot.

The car analogy: approaching a red light, you brake harder the closer you are (P) and ease off as your speed drops (D).

Why does a P-only controller leave a permanent error?

Take the mass–spring system with m = 1, k = 1 and u = K_p (r - x). At rest, the spring force must balance the controller's push: k x = K_p (r - x), so x = \frac{K_p}{k + K_p}\,r. With K_p = 1 the mass stops at half the reference; K_p = 4 gives 0.8\,r, K_p = 9 gives 0.9\,r. A P controller needs a nonzero error to produce any output at all, so it can never sit exactly at the target when something (here the spring) pushes back. The integral term fixes this: it keeps growing while any error remains, so the only resting point is e = 0 (checked by simulation: with K_p = 4 the mass stops at 0.8; adding K_i = 2 brings it to 1.0).

Worked example — reading the damping ratio
  1. Given: m = 1\,\mathrm{kg}, k = 4\,\mathrm{N/m}, c = 2\,\mathrm{N\,s/m}.
  2. Natural frequency: \omega_n = \sqrt{k/m} = 2\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}.
  3. Damping ratio: \zeta = \frac{c}{2 m \omega_n} = \frac{2}{2 \cdot 1 \cdot 2} = 0.5.
  4. Classify: \zeta < 1 → underdamped: it overshoots and oscillates while settling. \zeta = 1 (critically damped, c = 4) is the fastest response without overshoot; \zeta > 1 (overdamped) is sluggish.
Connection

The mass–spring–damper is the damped oscillator from 4 Oscillations and Waves. Tuning a PID controller amounts to choosing the effective spring (K_p) and damper (K_d) of the closed loop.

Optimal control

Video example: https://youtu.be/J5A3QqRcIqc

Robot example

Think of a wheeled autonomous service robot travelling between two locations in an (indoor) factory. The environment and the path are known, but humans may randomly be in the robot's workspace.

  • What type of actuators does it need?
  • What sensors would you recommend?
  • What should the controller(s) do?
Worked example — one possible answer to slide 19
  1. Actuators: electric motors (DC or brushless with gearboxes) for the drive wheels (3 Actuators); maybe a steering motor.
  2. Sensors (2 Sensors): wheel encoders (odometry), an IMU, a laser scanner/LiDAR or ultrasonic sensors to detect people and obstacles, bumpers or safety edges as a last line of defence, maybe a camera.
  3. Controllers: a low-level closed loop for each wheel's speed (PID on encoder feedback); a path-following controller that keeps the robot on the known path; and a safety layer that slows down when a person is near and stops when someone is too close — with the highest priority.

Concept of control systems

  • State — the output produced by a robotic system, denoted x. It depends on its previous states, the stimulus (signals) applied to the actuators, and the physics of the environment. It can be anything: pose, speed, velocity, angular velocity, force, etc.
  • Estimate — robots cannot determine the exact state x, but they can estimate it with their sensors; estimates are denoted y. It is the robotic engineer's responsibility to select good enough sensors, or to calibrate them well, so that y \approx x.
  • Reference — the goal state we wish to achieve, denoted r.
  • Error — the difference between reference and estimate, denoted e.
  • Control signal — the stimulus produced by the controller, denoted u. It is applied to the actuators.
  • Dynamics — also called the system plant / system model. It describes how the system behaves under non-static conditions. Dynamics are affected by the environment, which may change (not always linearly): floor type (concrete/wood), air drag, slope, etc.
Common mistake

Treating the sensor reading as the true state: "the error is r - x". The controller never sees x, only the estimate y, so it works on e = r - y. A miscalibrated sensor therefore makes a perfectly tuned controller hold the wrong value — very precisely. That's why sensor choice and calibration are listed as part of control.

Multiple controllers

  • A robot can have one or more controllers for different purposes, e.g. one for cruise control, another for the linear motion of the robot hand, another for the rotation of the hand, etc.

  • We need controllers because the dynamics (system plant) vary with time:

    • through the operation of the robot, e.g. it moves on different ground materials or performs tasks in different poses;
    • it is required to understand the physics of the environment well.

Summarized key requirements

  • The controller should reduce the error towards zero, e = 0: it should bring the estimate to the reference, y = r.
  • Robust: it should not depend on things we don't know; if the robot's environment changes, the controller should adapt.
  • Stable: it should not go out of control.
  • Smooth in its movements.
  • Responsive: fast enough to bring the output to the reference within a satisfactory time.
Why can't one controller be fast, smooth and stable all at once?

They pull against each other. Responsiveness needs high gains (react strongly to small errors); high gains are what cause overshoot and oscillation — the K = 1.6 curve — and, pushed further, instability. Smoothness and stability need gentler gains or more damping, which makes the response slower — the K = 0.5 curve. Tuning is choosing the compromise the task needs (a welding robot wants smooth, a pick-and-place robot wants fast).

Summary

"In summary, we give a reference state to a controller. The controller also has a/multiple sensor feedbacks. The reference state and sensor feedback are used together to generate the control signal. This control signal is fed to the 'System'. The system dynamics determine how the system behaves to this control input. Hopefully, the 'System' will reach our desired reference state if the controller is well defined."

Real mobile robots

  • Until recently, robots were mainly used in "closed environments" with fixed tasks and more or less known (constant) environments.

  • In a real deployment the problem is more complex:

    • the world is changing;
    • robots update their knowledge about the environment — localization, mapping and navigation;
    • new decisions have to be made based on feedback from the environment;
    • motion planning is part of the mission re-planning loop.
  • How to deal with real-world complexity? Relax constraints and consider realistic assumptions.

Planning & control

Intuition

A path is the geometric route (which points, in which order); a trajectory adds timing (where to be when, hence velocities and accelerations). The controller only ever follows the trajectory — it doesn't know about the mission.
